# Use sonar-onboard

<!-- Generated by build_pack_guides.py from pack.json and the skills' own files. Edit those, not this. -->

Scaffold a repo for Sonar compliance — supports both **SonarQube server** (self-hosted) and **SonarCloud** (SaaS), user picks at setup time. Generates `sonar-project.properties` with language-correct source/test/coverage paths, a CI workflow that runs the scanner on every push and PR and blocks merge on quality-gate failure, and a README snippet documenting the gate. One-shot setup; pair with `sonar-review` for per-change feedback.

**Reach for it when** the user says "set up Sonar", "add SonarQube to this repo", "wire up SonarCloud", "set up the quality gate", or asks to make a project Sonar-compliant for the first time.

## Install it

```bash
npx skilldrop-cli install sonar-onboard                 # Claude Code, your user folder
npx skilldrop-cli install sonar-onboard --project       # Claude Code, this repo
npx skilldrop-cli install sonar-onboard --ide cursor    # or kiro, codex, antigravity, copilot
```

It is part of the Dev team pack: [`--pack dev-team`](../packs/use-the-dev-team-pack.md) installs it with its neighbours.

## Ask for it

Say it the way you would to a colleague. Requests like these route to it:

- "Set up Sonar for this repo"
- "Scaffold sonar-project.properties and the CI workflow"
- "Onboard this project onto SonarCloud with a blocking quality gate"
- "We want Sonar checks on every PR — configure it"

Requests like these belong to a different skill, so it shouldn't answer them:

- "Run the Sonar scan and tell me if the gate passes"
- "Adversarially review this diff for edge cases"
- "Gate my change with lint, tests, and the reviewer panel"

If another skill answers instead, ask for this one by name: "use sonar-onboard".

## Check what you get

A good result:

- **Properties file is keyed to the actual repo.** `sonar.projectKey`, `sonar.sources`, `sonar.tests`, and the coverage path must reflect what's on disk — not a generic example. A properties file that scans the wrong directories produces a green gate that means nothing.
- **The workflow blocks merge on gate failure.** A scan that runs but doesn't fail PRs is decoration. The `sonarqube-quality-gate-action` step is non-negotiable.
- **Coverage path exists or is marked TODO.** Pointing at a coverage file that the test step never produces gives Sonar 0% coverage and a false-failing gate. Either wire it up end-to-end or leave it explicit.
- **`fetch-depth: 0` in checkout.** Shallow clones break Sonar's new-code-period detection. The first scan will look fine; the next ten PRs will mis-attribute issues.
- **Secrets are referenced, never inlined.** No raw tokens or URLs in committed files. The token belongs in GitHub Secrets; the URL too, even though it's not technically secret — it keeps fork PRs from leaking the host.
- **README snippet tells the next contributor what the gate enforces.** "Sonar must pass" is not enough — list the conditions (no new bugs, no new vulnerabilities, coverage on new code ≥ X%, duplication ≤ Y%).

## Use something else when

- Repo already has a working `sonar-project.properties` and a CI workflow that runs the scanner. Use `sonar-review` for per-change feedback instead.
- User wants to disable rules or relax the gate to make a failing scan pass. That's a code-quality conversation, not a setup task — push back.
- User wants language-specific deep config (custom rule profiles, Sonar plugins, branch analysis tuning). Out of scope; point at [`reference.md`](../../../packs/dev-team/skills/sonar-onboard/reference.md) and the Sonar docs.
- User wants both SonarQube server *and* SonarCloud scanning the same repo. Pick one — running both means two gates, two histories, and two answers to "did the build pass?".
